promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Uses and dangers of EM waves

questions.q: Which sequence lists the electromagnetic spectrum in the correct order from longest wavelength to shortest wavelength?
options: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
Gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
Radio, infrared, microwave, visible, X-ray, ultraviolet, gamma
Microwave, radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, gamma, X-ray
questions.explain: Radio waves have the longest wavelength and gamma rays the shortest, giving the order radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

questions.q: What type of wave are all electromagnetic waves?
questions.explain: All electromagnetic waves are transverse waves, with oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

questions.q: What is the approximate speed of all electromagnetic waves travelling through a vacuum?
questions.explain: In a vacuum all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed of about 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

questions.q: Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum has the highest frequency?
questions.explain: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and therefore the highest frequency of all EM waves.

questions.q: Moving through the spectrum from radio waves towards gamma rays, how do the wavelength and frequency change?
questions.explain: Because the wave speed is constant, as the wavelength decreases from radio to gamma the frequency increases.

questions.q: In a vacuum, how does the speed of X-rays compare with the speed of radio waves?
options: They travel at the same speed
questions.explain: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, regardless of their frequency.

questions.q: A radio wave has a wavelength of 1500 m and travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Using v = f λ, what is its frequency?
questions.explain: Rearranging v = f λ gives f = v ÷ λ = (3 × 10⁸) ÷ 1500 = 2 × 10⁵ Hz.

questions.q: A microwave has a frequency of 3 × 10⁹ Hz and travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. What is its wavelength?
questions.explain: Rearranging v = f λ gives λ = v ÷ f = (3 × 10⁸) ÷ (3 × 10⁹) = 0.1 m.

questions.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used by a television remote control?
questions.explain: Television remote controls send their signals using infrared radiation.

questions.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used to sterilise surgical instruments and to treat cancer?
questions.explain: Gamma rays are used to sterilise medical equipment and, in radiotherapy, to kill cancer cells.

questions.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used to produce medical images of broken bones?
questions.explain: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, allowing bones to be imaged.

questions.q: What is a danger of over-exposure to ultraviolet radiation?
questions.explain: Ultraviolet radiation damages skin cells and increases the risk of skin cancer as well as eye damage.

questions.q: Which three parts of the electromagnetic spectrum are ionising and can damage living cells?
questions.explain: Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays carry enough energy to ionise atoms and damage living cells.

questions.q: Why can microwaves be used to heat food but can also harm body tissue?
options: They are absorbed by water molecules, causing heating
They ionise the atoms in food
They reflect off water without any effect
They travel faster than other EM waves
questions.explain: Microwaves are absorbed by water molecules, transferring energy that heats the water and any tissue containing it.

questions.q: What does the law of reflection state?
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The angle of incidence is greater than the angle of reflection
The angle of incidence equals the angle of refraction
The angle of reflection is always 90°
questions.explain: For a reflected ray the angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

questions.q: When measuring the angle of incidence and angle of reflection, from which line are the angles measured?
questions.explain: Angles of incidence, reflection and refraction are all measured between the ray and the normal, a line drawn perpendicular to the surface.

questions.q: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block. How does the ray change direction?
options: It bends away from the normal
It continues in a straight line
questions.explain: Light slows down when it enters the denser glass, so the ray refracts towards the normal.

questions.q: A ray of light passes from glass into air, meeting the surface at an angle. In which direction does the ray bend as it leaves the glass?
questions.explain: Light speeds up as it enters the less dense air, so the ray refracts away from the normal.

questions.q: A converging lens is also correctly described as which type of lens?
questions.explain: A converging lens is a convex lens, which is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays to a focus.

questions.q: An object 2 cm tall produces an image 6 cm tall through a lens. Using magnification = image height ÷ object height, what is the magnification?
questions.explain: Magnification = image height ÷ object height = 6 ÷ 2 = 3, and magnification has no units.
